\section[il litigio]{il litigio — argument, quarrel}

\label{lesson:IT-C499-litigio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to look after, then the Italian for to obey.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il litigio}
\textbf{il litigio} — \textquotedblleft{}argument, quarrel\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Abbiamo avuto un litigio per i soldi.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We had an argument about money.}
\end{quote}

The noun for \emph{litigare}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{litigio} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{lītigium} \textquotedblleft{}a quarrel\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{lītigāre} \textquotedblleft{}to dispute\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{līs, lītis} \textquotedblleft{}a lawsuit\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il litigio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il litigio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il litigio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to look after, then the Italian for to obey, then say \emph{il litigio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il litigio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Argument, quarrel\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[riconciliarsi]{riconciliarsi — to make up, to be reconciled}

\label{lesson:IT-C499-riconciliarsi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to obey, then the Italian for argument.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: riconciliarsi}
\textbf{riconciliarsi} — \textquotedblleft{}to make up, to be reconciled\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dopo il litigio ci siamo riconciliati.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the argument we made up.}
\end{quote}

In speech \emph{fare pace} is more common.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{riconciliarsi} comes from Latin \emph{reconciliāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bring together again\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{conciliāre} \textquotedblleft{}to unite\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{riconciliarsi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{riconciliarsi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{riconciliarsi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to obey, then the Italian for argument, then say \emph{riconciliarsi} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does riconciliarsi mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To make up, to be reconciled\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tradire]{tradire — to betray; to cheat on}

\label{lesson:IT-C499-tradire}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for argument, then the Italian for to make up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tradire}
\textbf{tradire} — \textquotedblleft{}to betray; to cheat on\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Si sentiva tradita dalla sua migliore amica.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She felt betrayed by her best friend.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tradire il partner} — to be unfaithful. An \emph{-isc-} verb: \emph{tradisco}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tradire} is inherited from Latin \emph{trādere} \textquotedblleft{}to hand over, to betray\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tradire}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tradire}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{tradire}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for argument, then the Italian for to make up, then say \emph{tradire} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[la fedeltà]{la fedeltà — faithfulness, loyalty}

\label{lesson:IT-C499-fedelta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to make up, then the Italian for to betray.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la fedeltà}
\textbf{la fedeltà} — \textquotedblleft{}faithfulness, loyalty\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Per me la fedeltà è importante in una coppia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{For me faithfulness is important in a couple.}
\end{quote}

The adjective is \emph{fedele}; the wedding ring is \emph{la fede}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fedeltà} is inherited from Latin \emph{fidēlitātem} \textquotedblleft{}faithfulness\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{fidēs} \textquotedblleft{}trust\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to make up, then the Italian for to betray, then say \emph{la fedeltà} again

\section[confidarsi]{confidarsi — to confide (in someone)}

\label{lesson:IT-C499-confidarsi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to betray, then the Italian for faithfulness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: confidarsi}
\textbf{confidarsi} — \textquotedblleft{}to confide (in someone)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi confido solo con mia sorella.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I only confide in my sister.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Confidarsi con qualcuno}. A secret you tell is \emph{una confidenza}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{confidarsi} is usually traced to Vulgar Latin \emph{cōnfīdāre}, from Latin \emph{cōnfīdere} \textquotedblleft{}to trust fully\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{fīdere} \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{confidarsi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{confidarsi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to betray, then the Italian for faithfulness, then say \emph{confidarsi} again
\end{itemize}
